In everyday speech, it’s often conjugated (e.g., 여기 있어요/있어), but the dictionary form “여기 있다” is common in writing, captions, or emphatic statements.
native_language_example: I’m here.

additional_notes: Literally “(it) exists/is here” (여기 = here, 있어 = is/exists). The subject is often omitted, so it can mean either “I’m here” (answering a call, showing your presence) or “It’s here” (showing an object’s location). Used as a question to check presence: “여기 있어?” = “Are you here?” / “Is it here?” It can also be used like “Anyone here…?”: “~ 할 줄 아는 사람 여기 있어?” = “Is there anyone here who can…?” Polite versions: 여기 있어요 / 여기 있습니다.
native_language_example: The wallet is here!

meaning: “even if (I) stay here / even if (I’m) here”.
additional_notes: Often used right before 되다 to ask for permission: 여기 있어도 돼요?/되나요? = “Is it okay if I stay here?” / “Can I be here?” Here 여기 = “here”, 있다 = “to be/stay”, and -아/어도 = “even if / even though / even when”. The politeness level depends on the ending (돼요/되나요 polite, 되니 casual, 되죠 seeking agreement).
native_language_example: Is it okay if I stay here for a moment?

additional_notes: Literally “(to) be here” (여기 = here, 있어요 = is/are/have). Used to say someone/something is present in this place (“He’s still here.”), or when handing/finding something to mean “Here it is.” Subject is often omitted from context (e.g., 저 여기 있어요 = “I’m here!”). Polite, everyday speech style.
native_language_example: The wallet is here.

meaning: “if (someone) is here / if you stay here”.
additional_notes: 여기 = “here” + 있다 = “to be/stay” + -(으)면 = “if/when”. The subject is often omitted, so it can mean “if I/you/he/she/they am/are/is here.” Very commonly followed by 안 돼/안 돼요 (“mustn’t/can’t”), as in 여기 있으면 안 돼 = “You can’t stay here / You mustn’t be here.”
native_language_example: If you stay here, it’s dangerous.

meaning: “Here, please…” / “Over here, please…” (a polite attention-getter or softener).
additional_notes: Literally “here” + “a bit,” but it’s commonly used to soften a request or to draw attention to a place/person. Often followed by a request: 여기 좀 도와줘요 (Help me here), 여기 좀 봐 주세요 (Look here), 여기 좀 앉아도 될까요? (May I sit here?). In casual speech you may also hear 여기 좀요 / 여기 좀 봐요.
native_language_example: Please look here.

meaning: "what (are you) doing here / what do you want to do here".
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question meaning “what … here?”. Often followed by a verb like 하다 (do), 할 거야? (are you going to do?), 하고 싶어? (want to do). 뭘 is a common contraction of 무엇을 (“what” as an object). Depending on tone/context, it can sound neutral (“What do you want to do here?”) or suspicious/accusatory (“What are you doing here?”).
native_language_example: What are you looking for here right now?

meaning: "What are you doing here?" / "What are you doing (here)?"
additional_notes: Used to question what someone is doing in this place (여기서 = "here"). It’s often said with surprise, suspicion, or confusion, especially when the person seems out of place (e.g., late at night: "이 새벽에 여기서 뭐 해?"). Common expansions include "여기서 뭐 해?" (casual), "여기서 뭐 해요?" (polite), and "여기서 뭐 하고 있어? / 뭐 하는 거야?" (asking what they’re doing right now).
target_language_example: 지금 여기서 뭐 해요? 다들 기다리고 있어요.
native_language_example: What are you doing here right now? Everyone is waiting.

meaning: "What are you doing here?" / "What are you doing (here)?"
additional_notes: A casual, spoken phrase that usually continues with 있어(요)? (e.g., "여기서 뭐 하고 있어?" / "여기서 뭐 하고 있어요?"). 여기서 means "here" (at this place), and 뭐 하고 comes from "뭐 하다" (to do what). Often used when you’re surprised to see someone or are asking what they’re up to in this place.
native_language_example: What are you doing here?

meaning: “What are you doing here?” / “Why are you here?”
additional_notes: Used when you see someone in a place and ask what they’re doing there. Commonly followed by 하다: 여기서 뭐 해? (casual), 여기서 뭐 하냐? (more blunt/rough), 여기서 뭐 해요? (polite). Depending on tone and context, it can sound surprised, suspicious, or confrontational (especially with insults like 이 새끼).
native_language_example: What are you doing here right now?

additional_notes: A common fragment meaning “what” (뭘 = 뭐를, “what” + object marker) with “here” (여기서, “here/at this place”). It’s usually followed by a verb like 하다 (do), 먹다 (eat), etc. With words like 대체/도대체 (“the heck/on earth”), it often sounds surprised, annoyed, or scolding: “What the heck are you doing here?” In polite questions it can be neutral: “Is it okay if I eat something here?”
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do here.

meaning: "How did you get here?" / "What brings you here?"
additional_notes: Short for 여기는 어떻게 (“as for here, how…?”). It’s commonly used as the start of a question like 여긴 어떻게 왔어/왔어요? (“How did you come here?”). By itself (여긴 어떻게?) it’s an elliptical question where the verb (e.g., 왔어/왔어요) is understood from context. The politeness level is shown by the ending you add: 왔소? (very formal/old-fashioned), 왔어요? (polite), 왔어? / 왔지? (casual).
native_language_example: How did you get here?

meaning: “What brings you here…?” / “What are you doing here…?” (often said with surprise).
additional_notes: Shortened from “여기는” (as for here) + “어쩐” (“what kind of/what”). It’s usually followed by a noun like “일” (situation/occasion): “여긴 어쩐 일이지?” = “What brings you here?” Similar patterns: “여긴 어쩐 바람이 불어서 왔어?” (“What made you come here?”).
native_language_example: What brings you here?

meaning: “Why are you here?” / “What brings you here?”
additional_notes: 여긴 is a contraction of 여기는 (“as for here / here”). Used to ask the reason someone is here or came here, often followed by a verb like 왔어/왔어요/왔소 (“came”) or 온 거야 (“did you come”). It can also be said alone (여긴 왜?) when the rest is understood from context.
native_language_example: Why did you come here?

additional_notes: A strong, aggressive insult used when you’re very angry at someone. Literally means “eat yeot (Korean taffy),” but it’s an idiomatic curse and not used in polite conversation. Avoid using it; you may hear it in fights, movies, or online comments.
target_language_example: 나한테 다시는 말 걸지 마. 엿 먹어.
native_language_example: Don’t ever talk to me again. Fuck you.

additional_notes: A very offensive command literally meaning “eat yeot (Korean taffy).” Used to insult someone or tell them to go away. Not appropriate in polite conversation; avoid using it unless you understand the social consequences.
target_language_example: 나한테 다시 연락하지 마. 엿 먹어라.
native_language_example: Don’t contact me again. Fuck you.

meaning: to go (somewhere) to watch a movie.
additional_notes: "보러" is from "보다" (to watch/see) + "-러" (in order to). It’s commonly used with 가다/가요/갈까/가자 (to go): "영화 보러 가요" = "I’m going to watch a movie" (lit. go in order to watch a movie). You can also replace "영화" with another activity: "밥 먹으러" (to go eat), "커피 마시러" (to go drink coffee).
native_language_example: Do you want to go watch a movie together this weekend?

additional_notes: 영화( movie ) + -(를) object marker + 보다( to see/watch ). The dictionary form is 영화를 보다; in real conversations it’s commonly conjugated (e.g., 영화를 봐요/봤어요/볼까요?). Use this exact form in writing, titles, or when citing the verb phrase itself.
native_language_example: I watch a movie every weekend.

additional_notes: Used when giving an example or asking someone to give one. Often followed by a noun or a full sentence: “예를 들면 A요/예를 들면 A가 있어요.” In conversation it can be used alone as a prompt/question (“예를 들면?”) meaning “For example?” or “Like what?”.
native_language_example: For example, what kind of food do you like?

meaning: (Someone) is coming / is on the way.
additional_notes: Casual present-progressive form of 오다 (“to come”), from -고 있다 (“to be doing”). Often used as an urgent warning or update: “They’re coming!” You can add a subject/topic: 엄마가 오고 있어 (“Mom’s coming”). Polite equivalents: 오고 있어요, 오고 있습니다.
native_language_example: The taxi is coming right now.

additional_notes: From 오다 (“to come”) + -는 거야, a common spoken pattern used to ask for confirmation or to explain a situation. Often used as a question with rising intonation: 오는 거야? (“Are you coming?”). With 안: 안 오는 거야? (“You’re not coming?” / “Are you not coming?”). In context it can also mean “Is it coming?” (e.g., a bus, food, a package).
native_language_example: Are you coming home now?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the night of today (often including this evening). Common for making plans or confirming timing: 오늘 밤 뭐 해요? (“What are you doing tonight?”). Can be used alone as a surprised/confirming question: 오늘 밤? (“Tonight?”).
native_language_example: Do you have time tonight?

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or availability later today, typically in the evening or at night. 오늘 = today, 밤 = night, -에 marks the time (“on/at”). Often used in questions about schedules: 오늘 밤에 시간 돼? (Are you free tonight?)
native_language_example: Do you want to watch a movie tonight?

meaning: "the one from today" / "that kid (I mean) today".
additional_notes: 오늘 = “today,” 얘 = an informal way to say “this kid/this person/this one” (often used about someone younger, a friend, or someone you’re speaking casually about). Put together, 오늘 얘 refers to the person/thing you’re talking about in connection with today (e.g., “the kid who was here today,” “the one we met today”). Because 얘 is casual, this phrase is informal; in more polite speech you might say 오늘 그 사람(요) (“that person today”).
native_language_example: What was the name of that kid/person from today again?

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans for later today, typically after late afternoon. Often appears with questions about what to do, where to go, or where to sleep/stay (e.g., 오늘 저녁 뭐 해? 오늘 저녁 어디서 자?). Similar to 오늘 밤 (“tonight/night”), but 오늘 저녁 focuses more on the evening time (often including dinner time).
native_language_example: Do you want to eat together tonight?

additional_notes: From the verb 걸리다 (“to take (time) / to require”). 오래 걸려 is casual/plain style; polite is 오래 걸려요. Often used when asking why something is taking so long, with the subject omitted (e.g., cooking, eating, waiting, travel time).
native_language_example: Does it take a long time to get home from here?

additional_notes: A polite, formal welcome used to greet someone who has arrived (often with a place: “~에/으로 오신 것을 환영합니다” = “Welcome to ~”). “다시 오신 것을 환영합니다” means “Welcome back.” Built from 오다 (to come) + honorific -시- + 것 (the fact of) + 환영하다 (to welcome).
native_language_example: Welcome to our café.

additional_notes: Imperative negative form of 오다 (to come): 오- + -지 마 = “don’t do it.” Often used as a warning or to tell someone not to approach. Commonly paired with 가까이 (closely) or 이쪽으로 (this way/over here): 가까이 오지 마! “Don’t come closer!” / 이쪽으로 오지 마! “Don’t come this way!” Can sound strong/urgent depending on tone; more polite alternatives include 오지 마세요 or 오지 말아 주세요.
native_language_example: It’s dangerous, so don’t come here!

additional_notes: A negative command built from 오다 (to come) + -지 말다 (don’t…). In real speech it’s usually conjugated (오지 마 / 오지 마요 / 오지 마세요), but the dictionary/citation form is 오지 말다. You can also use it in reported speech: 오지 말라고 했어요 = “I told (them) not to come.”
native_language_example: To not come to my house today.

additional_notes: Spoken contraction of **온 것이야**: **오다** (to come) + **-(으)ㄴ 것** (the fact that…) + **이야/야** (casual ‘to be’). Often used in questions to ask why/how someone came, or to confirm someone’s arrival: **왜 온 거야?** (Why did you come?), **메리도 온 거야?** (Did Mary come too?). With places: **여길/여기에 온 거야?** (Did you come here?). With **갔다 온 거야** it means “went and came back” → “Where did you go?” in natural English.
native_language_example: Did you come here just now?

additional_notes: 온 is the past attributive form of 오다 (to come), so it modifies a following noun. 걸 is a common spoken contraction of 것을 (object form of 것, “thing/fact”). So 온 걸 often appears in longer sentences like ~온 걸 알아요 (“I know that ~ came”) or ~온 걸 후회해요 (“I regret that I came”). In writing, you may also see 온 것을.
native_language_example: I regret coming here.

additional_notes: Casual/intimate future form of 오다 (“to come”). It’s short for "올 거야" = "올 거(것)야" (literally “it is a thing that [someone] will come”). Used to state an expectation/plan (“He’ll come”) or to ask about it (“Will you come?”). For polite speech, use "올 거예요?" / "올 거예요."
native_language_example: Even if I'm a little late, I’ll definitely come.

additional_notes: From the verb 오다 (to come) + -(으)ㄹ 거예요, a common future form meaning “will/going to.” Used to ask or say that someone is expected to come in the future (often near future). It can be a statement (올 거예요.) or a question (올 거예요?). Polite style; informal versions include 올 거야 / 올 거예요? → 올 거야?
native_language_example: I’ll come home at 7 o’clock.

additional_notes: From 오다 (to come) + -(으)ㄹ 거지? which asks for confirmation or expects agreement (similar to a tag question). It’s casual/informal speech, often used with friends or people younger than you. In full form you may hear 올 거지?, 올 거야?, or 올 거죠? (more polite). Often used with a time/place implied by context (e.g., ‘to the meeting / to my house’).
native_language_example: You’re coming tomorrow too, right?

meaning: 'be able to come' / 'can come' (used with 있다/없다).
additional_notes: From 오다 (to come) + -(으)ㄹ 수 (ability/possibility). It’s not usually used alone—you normally say 올 수 있어요/있어? (can you come?) or 올 수 없어요 (I can’t come). Often used to ask if someone is available to come now or to an event.
target_language_example: 내일 우리 집에 올 수 있어요?
native_language_example: Can you come to my place tomorrow?

meaning: to wear clothes; to get dressed.
additional_notes: 옷(“clothes”) + 을(object marker) + 입다(“to wear/put on (clothing)”). Often used in polite speech as 옷을 입어요 (“I’m getting dressed / I’m wearing clothes”). For specific items, you can replace 옷 with the clothing word: 셔츠를 입다 (wear a shirt), 코트를 입다 (wear a coat). Korean also uses different verbs for other things you “wear”: 신다 (shoes/socks), 쓰다 (hats/helmets), 끼다 (gloves/rings).
native_language_example: Every morning, I get dressed.

meaning: "Why did you go?" / "Why did you leave?" (informal).
additional_notes: A casual question asking the reason someone went somewhere or left. 왜 = why, 갔어 = (you) went (past tense of 가다). More polite versions: 왜 갔어요? / 왜 가셨어요? You can add a destination: 왜 집에 갔어? (Why did you go home?).
native_language_example: Why did you go? / Why did you leave?

meaning: "Why that…?" / "Why (do you) … like that?" (used before a noun or topic).
additional_notes: A common spoken chunk: 왜 (why) + 그 (that/the). It’s often followed by a noun: 왜 그 모양이야? (“Why do you look like that?/Why that appearance?”), 왜 그 얘기는… (“Why that story/topic…?”), 왜 그 이름을… (“Why that name…?”). Similar patterns: 왜 그랬어? (“Why did you do that?”) and 왜 그래? (“Why are you like that?/What’s wrong?”).
native_language_example: Why did you say that?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask why someone did/said/has something. 그걸 is a contraction of 그것을 (“that/it” + object marker 을/를). It’s typically followed by a verb, e.g. 왜 그걸 말해요? (“Why do you say that?”), 왜 그걸 샀어요? (“Why did you buy that?”).
native_language_example: Why are you saying that now?

meaning: “What’s wrong?” / “What’s up?” (why are you like that?)
additional_notes: A very common casual question used when someone seems upset, acting strangely, or you’re concerned about them. It can be caring (“Are you okay?”) or sound a bit scolding/annoyed depending on tone. Often followed by a name: “라몬, 왜 그래?” You can add emphasis like “무섭게 왜 그래?” = “Why are you being so scary like that?”
native_language_example: What’s wrong? Is something going on?

additional_notes: A casual way to ask why someone is acting a certain way or why something seems off (their face, mood, behavior, situation). Depending on tone, it can sound concerned ("Are you okay?") or annoyed/scolding ("What’s your problem?"). Politer: 왜 그래요? More blunt: 왜 그래? (to close friends).
target_language_example: 오늘 기분이 안 좋아 보여. 왜 그래?
native_language_example: You look like you’re in a bad mood today. What’s wrong?

meaning: "Why should I (do that)?" / "Why do I have to?"
additional_notes: Used to question or push back against a request/expectation, often with a frustrated or doubtful tone. It’s usually followed by an ending like 해(요)/하지/하죠/되죠, and the subject (often 내가 “I”) is frequently implied: (내가) 왜 그래야 해요? = “Why do I have to do that?”
target_language_example: 그걸 꼭 지금 해야 해요? 제가 왜 그래야 해요?
native_language_example: Do I really have to do that now? Why should I?

meaning: “What’s wrong?” / “Why are you acting like that?” (polite)
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone is behaving a certain way or what’s bothering them. Depending on tone, it can sound concerned ("Are you okay?") or slightly scolding ("Why are you doing that?"). Often followed by a name or title (e.g., 왜 그래요, 형님?). Informal version: 왜 그래?
native_language_example: Are you okay? What’s wrong?

meaning: “Why did you do that?” / “Why did you do it?”
additional_notes: Casual (해체) past-tense question, often said with surprise, frustration, or scolding after someone did something you didn’t expect. Literally “Why (was it) like that?” but in context it usually means “Why did you do that?” Politer versions: 왜 그랬어요? / 왜 그러셨어요?
target_language_example: 갑자기 나가 버리면 어떡해? 왜 그랬어?
native_language_example: Why would you just leave suddenly? Why did you do that?

meaning: "why (are you/they) doing that / being like that".
additional_notes: Used when asking the reason for someone’s behavior, mood, or the way someone is treating you (often because it seems strange, rude, or unexpected). It’s usually followed by a noun like 거야/거죠/건가 (e.g., 왜 그러는 거야? “Why are you doing that?”). The subject is often implied (“you”), but it can be made explicit: 라몬이 왜 그러는 거죠? “Why is Ramon acting like that?”
native_language_example: Why are you acting like that today?

additional_notes: A casual question (often to a child, friend, or someone you’re close to) asking why someone is acting a certain way or what the problem is. It can sound concerned (“What’s wrong?”) or mildly scolding depending on tone. More formal alternatives include “왜 그래요?” or “왜 그러세요?”
target_language_example: 얼굴이 안 좋아 보이는데, 왜 그러니?
native_language_example: You don’t look well—what’s wrong?

meaning: "What's wrong?" / "Why are you doing/acting like that?" (polite).
additional_notes: A polite way to ask why someone is behaving strangely or what the problem is. Often used when someone seems upset, surprised, or unwell. You can also specify a body part: "손이 왜 그러세요?" = "What’s wrong with your hand?". Less formal: "왜 그래?".
target_language_example: 얼굴이 안 좋아 보이는데, 왜 그러세요?
native_language_example: You don’t look well—what’s wrong?

additional_notes: Used to question the reason for something, often with a following noun: 왜 그런 + N (“why such a/an N?”). Common with things like 건/거 (“thing/situation”), 눈 (“look/eyes”), 소리 (“thing to say/remark”). Tone depends on the ending (e.g., 왜 그런 거예요? polite, 왜 그런 거야? casual).
native_language_example: Why did you say that?

meaning: “Why would you say that?” / “Why say such a thing?”
additional_notes: Used to question or react to what someone just said, often with surprise, hurt, or disbelief. It’s usually followed by a verb like 하다 (“to say/do”): 왜 그런 말을 해(요)? (present), 왜 그런 말을 했어(요)? (past). By itself (왜 그런 말을?) it’s an abbreviated, conversational “Why would you say that?”
target_language_example: 왜 그런 말을 했어? 난 상처받았어.
native_language_example: Why would you say that? I’m hurt.

meaning: 'Why did you do something like that?' (why such a bad/strange act?)
additional_notes:
Used to question (often criticize) someone’s behavior: “Why would you do that?” 
- 왜 = why
- 그런 = like that / such
- 짓 = an act/deed (often negative when used like this: “a bad thing to do”)
Usually followed by 하다 in a specific form: 왜 그런 짓을 해? / 했어? / 하는 거야? / 하세요? / 해야 하죠?
More polite: 왜 그런 짓을 하세요? / 왜 그런 짓을 해야 하죠? 
More casual: 왜 그런 짓을 해?
native_language_example: Why did you do something like that?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s behavior, attitude, way of doing something, or opinion. 그렇게 means “like that / in that way,” and adding 왜 makes it “why like that / why so…”. Often used with verbs and adjectives (e.g., 왜 그렇게 오래 걸려? “Why does it take so long?”). Depending on tone/context, it can sound neutral or slightly critical (similar to “Why are you being like that?”).
native_language_example: Why are you so quiet today?

meaning: "Why (to/at) me?" / "Why are you doing/saying that to me?"
additional_notes: Used to complain or question why someone is directing an action, attitude, or words at you. Often followed by a verb like 그래/이래("act like that"), 난리야("make a fuss"), 말 안 했어("didn't tell me"), etc. Because it uses 나 (casual “I/me”), it’s informal; in polite speech, say 왜 저한테.
native_language_example: Why are you only like that to me?

additional_notes: 왜 = 'why'. 날 is a contraction of 나를 ('me' with the object marker -를). It’s used when 'me' is the direct object of the verb: 왜 날 도와줘? ('Why are you helping me?'), 왜 날 봐? ('Why are you looking at me?'). Often the verb is understood from context, so you may hear incomplete-sounding questions like 왜 날 여기에…? meaning 'Why (bring) me here?' or 'Why am I here?'.
native_language_example: Why are you treating me like this?

additional_notes: 왜 = “why,” 내 = “my.” This is usually the start of a longer question, often sounding like “Why don’t you…?” when followed by a negative verb: 왜 내 말(을) 안 들어? (“Why don’t you listen to me?”). Common patterns: 왜 내 말 안 들어? (listen to what I say), 왜 내 말을 안 믿어? (believe what I say). 내 is the casual form of “my” (formal: 제). Often you’ll see object particles attached: 내 말**을**, 내 사진**을**.
native_language_example: Why don’t you believe what I’m saying?

additional_notes: 왜 = “why,” and 내가 = “I” (subject). Used to question or protest that *you* should do something, or to express confusion about why something involves you. It’s often followed by a verb (e.g., 왜 내가 가? “Why would I go?”) and can also stand alone as 왜 내가? meaning “Why me?” The subject marker -가 is included because the speaker is emphasizing “me/I.”
native_language_example: Why do I have to do that?

additional_notes: 왜 = “why.” 널 is the contracted form of 너를 (“you” + object marker 를) used in casual speech/writing. It commonly appears before a verb to mean “why (should/would) I do [verb] to/for you?” (e.g., 왜 널 도와야 해? “Why should I help you?”).
native_language_example: Why should I trust you?

additional_notes: Used to ask why a whole group of people is doing something. 왜 = "why"; 다들 (short for 다들 = "everyone/all of you") adds the feeling of "everyone" or "all" (often with a sense of "everyone, in general"). Common pattern: 왜 다들 + (verb/adjective)? e.g., 왜 다들 조용해? "Why is everyone so quiet?" It can sound complaining, surprised, or confused depending on tone and context.
native_language_example: Why is everyone (you all) so late?

additional_notes: A fragment that commonly appears in questions like "왜 당신을 괴롭히지?" = "Why does that bother you?" Here, "왜" means "why" and "당신을" means "you" with the object particle -(으)ㄹ. In everyday Korean, "당신" can sound confrontational when used to mean "you" (especially between strangers or in arguments), so Koreans often prefer someone’s name/title (e.g., "왜 민수 씨를…", "왜 선생님을…") or omit "you" when it’s obvious.
target_language_example: 그 말이 왜 당신을 화나게 해요?
native_language_example: Why does that comment make you angry?

meaning: 'Why (didn't) you say/tell (me)?' (used in 왜 말 안 해요? / 왜 말 안 했어?)
additional_notes: 왜 = “why” and 말(하다) = “to say/tell/speak.” It’s most commonly used as part of the complaint/question pattern “왜 말 안 해(요)?” = “Why aren’t you telling me?” / “Why didn’t you say so?” Often implies the speaker expected the other person to mention something earlier. Politeness changes with endings: 말 안 해요? (polite), 말 안 했어? (casual), 말 안 했죠? (softer/polite, often expecting agreement).
target_language_example: 중요한 일이면 왜 말 안 했어요?
native_language_example: If it was important, why didn’t you tell me?

additional_notes: Short for 왜 말 안 해(요)/했어(요)? (“Why aren’t/didn’t you say anything?”). 말 안 하다 literally means “to not say (it)” / “to not tell (someone).” It’s normally followed by a verb ending like 해?, 했어?, 한 거야?, 했죠?, 했을까요? The listener/context fills in what wasn’t said (and often who it wasn’t told to).
target_language_example: 왜 말 안 했어요? 저도 알았으면 좋았을 텐데요.
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me? It would’ve been nice if I’d known too.

meaning: "Why don’t you…?" / "Why aren’t you…?" (used before a verb; literally “why + 말 + not”).
additional_notes:
This is an unfinished fragment that normally continues with a verb, like:
- 왜 말을 안 해요? = Why aren’t you talking?
- 왜 말을 안 들어? = Why don’t you listen?
- 왜 말을 안 탔어요? = Why didn’t you ride the horse?

Be careful: 말 can mean “words/speaking” or “horse,” so the meaning depends on the following verb (하다/듣다 vs 타다).
native_language_example: Why aren’t you talking?

additional_notes: 왜 = “why,” 못 = “can’t” (inability) / “not allowed to” (restriction), depending on context. It’s typically followed by a verb (e.g., 못 나가다 “can’t go out,” 못 나오다 “can’t come out,” 못 보다 “can’t see/watch”). In conversation the subject is often omitted, so it can mean “Why can’t I…?” or “Why can’t you…?”
native_language_example: Why can’t you go in?

additional_notes: Used to ask (often with surprise, impatience, or concern) why a situation hasn’t changed yet. 왜 = “why”, 아직도 = “still / even now”. Commonly followed by a verb phrase like 일하고 있어(요) “are working”, 학교에 있어(요) “are at school”.
native_language_example: Why are you still not sleeping?

additional_notes: Used to ask why something is not happening or why someone isn’t doing something. Pattern: 왜 안 + verb? (e.g., 왜 안 와? “Why aren’t you coming?”). Can sound like a complaint or impatience depending on tone and context.
native_language_example: Why aren’t you coming? Where are you now?

additional_notes: A common question pattern: 왜 (why) + 여기 (here). Often followed by a verb like 있어요/있죠 (to be here), 있는데 (are here/there is), 살지 (live), 없죠 (not here). It can sound surprised or questioning depending on tone and context.
native_language_example: Why are you coming here? / Why are you here?

meaning: “Why is (someone/I) here?” / “What am I/are they doing here?”
additional_notes: A casual, slightly puzzled question used when you unexpectedly find someone (or yourself) in a place. Often implies surprise or confusion (“How come they’re here?”). The subject is frequently omitted when obvious from context (e.g., just 왜 여기 있지?). With a name/person: “래리가 왜 여기 있지?” = “Why is Larry here?”
native_language_example: Why am I here?

additional_notes: A common question starter: 왜 (why) + 여기 (here) + 에 (to/in). Usually followed by a verb like 와(요)? (come?), 있어(요)? (be?), 있니? (casual), 있죠? (polite). It can also be used on its own as a short, surprised question (e.g., in a hospital: “This patient—why here?”).
native_language_example: Why did you come here?

meaning: "Why did you come?" / "What brings you here?" (casual).
additional_notes: Casual/informal question using the past tense of 오다 (to come): 오다 → 왔어. Often used when someone arrives and you’re asking their reason for coming. With a location/topic it can sound like “Why are you here?” (e.g., 여긴 왜 왔어?). Politer alternatives: 왜 왔어요? (polite), 왜 오셨어요? (more respectful).
native_language_example: Why did you come all of a sudden?

meaning: “Why did you come?” / “What brought you here?”
additional_notes: 왜 = “why,” 왔어요 = polite past form of 오다 (“to come”), often used when someone has arrived and you’re asking the reason/purpose for coming. You can add a place/topic before it: 여기 왜 왔어요? (“Why did you come here?”), 이 동네에 왜 왔어요? (“Why did you come to this neighborhood?”). Polite, everyday speech; for more formal use 왜 오셨어요?; informal casual is 왜 왔어?
native_language_example: Why did you come all of a sudden?

additional_notes: Used to question why something involves “us/we/our.” Often followed by a topic/subject marker (왜 우리는…, 왜 우리가…) or a noun (왜 우리 돈…, 왜 우리 회사…). In the example, 왜 우리 돈이 더 필요해? means “Why do we need more money?” (literally “Why does our money need to be more?”).
native_language_example: Why do only we have to do it?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for something involving “us” as the subject. 왜 = “why” and 우리가 = “we/us” + subject marker 가, emphasizing that *we* (not someone else) are doing/experiencing it. Often followed by a verb or a longer clause (e.g., 왜 우리가 사과해야 해? “Why do we have to apologize?”). In casual speech you may also hear 왜 우리가 → 왜 우리가요? / 왜 우리가 해야 해?
native_language_example: Why do we have to contact them first?

meaning: "Why are you crying?" / "Why are you (currently) crying?"
additional_notes: Usually appears as 왜 울고 있어? / 왜 울고 있어요? / 왜 울고 있나요? It’s 왜 (why) + 울다 (to cry) + -고 있다 (to be doing, ongoing action). On its own, 왜 울고… can sound unfinished, like you’re about to continue ("Why are you crying…?"). Use it to ask the reason someone is crying; add 있어요/있어 for the natural full question.
target_language_example: 무슨 일 있어? 왜 울고 있어?
native_language_example: Is something wrong? Why are you crying?

additional_notes: A casual/informal question: 왜 (“why”) + 울어 (from 울다, “to cry,” in 반말 style). Use with friends, kids, or someone younger. Polite alternatives: 왜 울어요? / 왜 우세요? (honorific). Often said with concern: “What’s wrong—why are you crying?”
native_language_example: Is something wrong? Why are you crying?

meaning: “why this/these …?” (why this person/thing, why these people, etc.)
additional_notes: Used when **왜 (why)** comes right before **이 (this/these)**, which modifies the following noun: **왜 이 사람… (why this person…)**, **왜 이 학교… (why this school…)**. It often sounds like you’re questioning or challenging the reason for choosing *this particular* person/thing. Spacing is often **왜 이** before a noun; in speech it’s said together.
native_language_example: Why do you want to go to this restaurant?

meaning: "What’s wrong?" / "Why are you like this?" (said when something seems strange, bad, or unexpected).
additional_notes: A common casual complaint/surprised reaction. You can say it to a person (넌 왜 이래? “What’s wrong with you?/Why are you acting like this?”) or about a thing/situation (이거 왜 이래? “What’s wrong with this?”). Often appears as X가/이 왜 이래? (e.g., 꼴이 왜 이래? “Why do you look like that?/What’s with this mess?”). Tone can sound annoyed depending on context.
native_language_example: What’s wrong with you today? / Why are you acting like this today?

additional_notes: A very common spoken phrase used when something seems weird, broken, or someone is acting strangely. The subject can be a thing (내 차는 왜 이래? “What’s wrong with my car?”) or a person/group (너 왜 이래? “What’s wrong with you?”). Often has an annoyed, confused, or complaining tone; adding 진짜 makes it stronger (“Seriously, what’s wrong?”). It’s a shortened form of 왜 이래(요)?; use 왜 이래요? to be more polite.
target_language_example: 오늘 너 왜 이래? 무슨 일 있어?
native_language_example: What’s wrong with you today? Is something going on?

meaning: "What’s wrong?" / "Why are you doing (acting) like this?"
additional_notes: Used when you’re surprised, annoyed, or worried about someone’s behavior or a situation. It can sound like a complaint (“What’s your problem?”) depending on tone, even though it ends politely with -요. Often said as a question: 왜 이래요? (“What’s wrong?”). You can add a subject for clarity, e.g., 다들 왜 이래요? (“What’s wrong with everyone?”).
target_language_example: 갑자기 왜 이래요? 무슨 일 있어요?
native_language_example: What’s wrong all of a sudden? Is something going on?

additional_notes: Used when you’re confused, upset, or surprised by someone’s behavior or by a situation. It’s usually followed by a noun like 거야/거냐/거지/거죠/건가 to form a full question: 왜 이러는 거야? (casual) / 왜 이러는 거죠? (polite). Often implies “What’s wrong?” or “Why are you being like this?” depending on context.
native_language_example: Why are you acting like this today?

meaning: “What’s wrong with you?” / “Why are you acting like this?”
additional_notes: A casual (반말) way to question someone’s strange, rude, or upsetting behavior, often with annoyance or concern. It can also mean “Why are you doing this (to me)?” depending on context (e.g., 나한테 왜 이러니?). Similar: 왜 이래?, 왜 그래?. More polite: 왜 이러세요?
target_language_example: 너 오늘 왜 이러니? 무슨 일 있어?
native_language_example: What’s wrong with you today? Did something happen?

meaning: “Why are you doing this?” / “What’s wrong?” (often said in surprise or to scold).
additional_notes: A polite(-ish) question using -세요, but it often sounds accusatory depending on tone and context (like “What’s your problem?”). Common when someone is acting strangely, being rude, or causing trouble. You can add a person/object: 저한테 왜 이러세요? (“Why are you doing this to me?”).
native_language_example: Why are you acting like this right now? Please calm down.

additional_notes: Used to complain or express disbelief, usually before a noun (e.g., 왜 이런 데… = “why a place like this…”, 왜 이런 짓… = “why (do) this kind of thing…”). It often sounds rhetorical, like you think the situation/action is strange or wrong. Can be used with past/present: 왜 이런 짓을 했어? (did), 왜 이런 짓을 하는 거야? (are doing).
native_language_example: Why are you saying something like that?

meaning: "Why so...?/Why is it like this?" (why so late/noisy/slow, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to ask (often with surprise, annoyance, or curiosity) why something is happening to such a strong degree. Pattern: 왜 이렇게 + adjective/verb? e.g., 왜 이렇게 늦었어? (Why are you so late?), 왜 이렇게 시끄러워? (Why is it so noisy?), 왜 이렇게 오래 걸렸어? (Why did it take so long?). In casual speech it can sound complaining.
native_language_example: Why are you so tired today?

additional_notes: Used to ask (often with surprise, annoyance, or criticism) why someone/something is to such a degree. It’s similar to 왜 이렇게, with 이리 meaning “like this/this much.” Commonly followed by an adjective or adverb: 왜 이리 시끄러? (so noisy), 왜 이리 오래 걸려? (take so long). Can also be used about frequency/behavior: 요즘 왜 이리 안 온 거야? (“Why haven’t you been coming lately?”).
native_language_example: Why do you look so tired today?

additional_notes: Used to complain or express surprise that someone is doing/saying something late or only now. Often followed by a verb like 말해요 (tell), 와/왔어 (come/came), 해요 (do). Can sound a bit annoyed depending on tone. Literally 'why now/why only now'.
native_language_example: Why are you only contacting me now?

meaning: "Why do you keep (doing that)?" / "Why do you keep on…?"
additional_notes: 왜 = “why” and 자꾸 = “repeatedly/again and again/keep (doing).” Together, 왜 자꾸 is used to question repeated behavior and often sounds annoyed, impatient, or frustrated depending on tone. It’s commonly followed by a verb: 왜 자꾸 물어? (“Why do you keep asking?”), 왜 자꾸 가려고 해? (“Why do you keep trying to go?”). In polite speech you may hear 왜 자꾸 물어요?; in casual speech, 왜 자꾸 물어?
native_language_example: Why do you keep calling (me)?

meaning: “What’s wrong with that (person/thing)?” / “Why is (he/she/it) like that?”
additional_notes: Used when you notice something strange, annoying, or unexpected about someone’s behavior or a situation/object. Very common in speech; 저래 is a contraction of 저러(다) (“to be like that”) + -어. Often appears as 쟤 왜 저래? (“What’s wrong with him/her?”). Can sound rude/judgmental depending on tone and the noun used (especially 저 인간은 왜 저래? which is quite insulting).
native_language_example: He’s suddenly getting angry—what’s wrong with him?

additional_notes: Casual question used to challenge the reason for an action or a remark. What’s being done/said is often understood from context: 그 얘기를 왜 해? (“Why say that?”), 그런 부탁을 왜 해? (“Why ask a favor like that?”). In polite speech you can say 왜 해요?
native_language_example: Why would you say something like that?

additional_notes: Used to ask why someone is alone or doing something alone, often implying surprise or concern. Commonly followed by a verb like 있어(요) (be/stay), 갔어 (went), or 해/했어 (do/did). You can omit the subject (너) because it’s understood from context. Polite version: 왜 혼자 … 있어요? Casual: 왜 혼자 … 있어?
native_language_example: Why did you come alone today?

additional_notes: From 울다 (to cry) + -(는) 거야, a very common spoken pattern that adds an explanatory/emphatic tone (often surprise, disbelief, or pressing for a reason). It’s often used as a question: 우는 거야? = “Are you crying?” / “You’re crying?” More polite: 우는 거예요? / 왜 우는 거예요? You’ll also hear 우는 거야? even when the speaker can already see tears, like “Wait, you’re actually crying?”
target_language_example: 지금 우는 거야? 무슨 일 있었어?
native_language_example: Are you crying right now? Did something happen?

additional_notes: 우리 = "we/our" (often also used to mean "my" in Korean, especially when talking about family). 가족 = "family". 은 is a topic particle attached to 가족 (가족은), used to set "my/our family" as the topic of the sentence and contrast it with others if needed. Common in neutral/polite speech; not slang.
target_language_example: 우리 가족은 주말에 같이 저녁을 먹어요.
native_language_example: My/our family eats dinner together on weekends.

additional_notes: Literally means “our son,” but in Korean 우리 (“we/our”) is commonly used to refer to one’s own close family member (so it can mean “my son”). It can be used to talk about your son (우리 아들은 어때요? “How is my son?”) or to call out to him directly like “Son!” (우리 아들!).
native_language_example: My son, how was school today?

additional_notes: Koreans very commonly say 우리 ("our") when talking about close family members (엄마, 아빠, 집, etc.) even when they mean "my." In speech, the possessive marker 의 is often omitted (우리 엄마 = 우리 엄마의). It can be used in casual or polite sentences depending on the verb endings (e.g., 보셨어요? is polite; 못 봤어요? is polite-casual).
native_language_example: My mom is at home right now.

additional_notes: 우리 means "we/our," but in everyday Korean it’s very common to say 우리 when talking about your own family or home (like "my house," "my mom"). 우리 집 can mean either "my place" or "our place" depending on context.
native_language_example: Do you want to come over to my place today?

additional_notes: 우리 = “we/our,” but in everyday Korean it’s often used to mean “my” (especially for family, home, team, etc.). 집 = “house/home.” 에 marks a location/direction: with 오다/가다 it means “to (someone’s) house,” and without a movement verb it can mean “at (someone’s) house.” In casual speech, “우리 집에?” can be a surprised repeat like “To my place?”
native_language_example: Do you want to come hang out at my place today?

additional_notes: “우리” means “we/us,” and “다” means “all.” Together, “우리 다” is used to include everyone in your group. It often comes before the verb (e.g., 우리 다 먹었어 = we all ate). Commonly used with 같이 (“together”): 우리 다 같이….
target_language_example: 주말에 우리 다 같이 공원에 가요.
native_language_example: This weekend, let’s all go to the park together.

additional_notes: 우리를 = 우리 (we/us) + 를 (object particle). It marks 'us' as the direct object of the verb (the one being taught, saved, seen, caught, etc.). Related forms: 우리가 (we, subject), 우리를 (us, object), 우리에게/우리한테 (to us). Note that 우리 can also mean 'my/our' depending on context, but 우리를 specifically means 'us' as an object.
native_language_example: They helped us.

additional_notes: Used to include everyone in the group the speaker belongs to (“we” + “all”). Often used for emphasis or solidarity, and can be followed by particles like -가/-는 (우리 모두가/우리 모두는). You may also hear 우리 모두 다 (“all of us, everyone”) for extra emphasis.
native_language_example: Let’s all go together.

meaning: "what did we..." / "what are we..." (often: "what did we do wrong?")
additional_notes: 우리가 = “we” (subject). 뭘 is a shortened form of 무엇을 (“what” as the object). It’s used to start questions like “What did we do?” or “What are we doing/going to do?”, often with a defensive or rhetorical tone (e.g., 우리가 뭘 했다고? = “What did we even do?”). The rest of the meaning comes from the following verb: 했다고 (did), 위해 (for), 할지 (what we’ll do).
target_language_example: 우리가 뭘 잘못했는데 그렇게 화를 내?
native_language_example: What did we do wrong for you to get that angry?

meaning: "How would we…?" / "How are we supposed to…?"
additional_notes: 우리가 = “we” (with the subject marker -가). 어떻게 = “how.” This often starts a question meaning “How can we…?” or “How would we know…?”, and it can be rhetorical (implying it’s hard or impossible). The politeness level is shown by the verb ending that follows (e.g., 알아? casual, 해야 하나요? polite).
target_language_example: 우리가 어떻게 여기까지 왔는지 기억이 안 나요.
native_language_example: I don’t remember how we got here.

additional_notes: Used to question the reason or necessity for something involving “we/us.” It often comes at the beginning of a question, followed by a verb phrase (e.g., 우리가 왜 가야 해요? “Why do we have to go?”). In casual speech, the rest of the sentence may be shortened if it’s obvious from context.
native_language_example: Why do we have to leave now?

additional_notes: 우리(we/us) + 랑(= with; casual form of 와/과) + 같이(together). Used to invite someone to join your group or to ask if someone will do something/go somewhere with you. More formal: 우리와 같이.
native_language_example: Do you want to eat dinner with us tonight?

additional_notes: 우리(we/us) + 와/과(with) + 함께(together). Use it to say someone does something together with your group. In speech you may also hear the shorter form "우리랑" (with us), e.g. "우리랑 같이 가요". "함께 하다" means "to do (it) together" and is commonly used as an invitation: "우리와 함께 하자."
target_language_example: 주말에 우리와 함께 영화 보러 갈래요?
native_language_example: Do you want to go watch a movie with us this weekend?

meaning: 'can’t (do something to) us' / 'unable to (verb) us' (e.g., 'can’t trust us').
additional_notes: 우릴 is a contracted, spoken form of 우리를 (“us” as the object). 못 is used before a verb to mean “can’t” or “unable to” (often implying inability rather than refusal). Common pattern: 우릴 못 + verb (우릴 못 믿다 = “can’t trust us”). In more formal writing/speech, you’ll often see 우리를 못 instead of 우릴 못.
native_language_example: Why can’t you trust us?

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Literally “luck is good.” Commonly used to say someone had a lucky situation or good timing. Often paired with the opposite phrase 운이 나쁘다 (“to be unlucky”). You can also say 운이 좋았어요 (past) for “I was lucky.”
target_language_example: 오늘은 운이 좋다. 자리가 바로 났어요.
native_language_example: I’m lucky today. A seat opened up right away.

meaning: 'know how to drive' (as in 운전할 줄 알다).
additional_notes: Usually used with 알다/모르다: **운전할 줄 알아요?** = “Do you know how to drive?” This is the common pattern **-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다** meaning “to know/not know how to do (something)” (a learned skill or ability). You can use it with other verbs too (e.g., 수영할 줄 알아요 = know how to swim).
native_language_example: I know how to drive a car.

additional_notes: A direct command: 움직이다 (“to move”) + -지 마 (“don’t”). Common in urgent situations (e.g., police, danger, holding still). It can sound strong/rude depending on context; a softer version is 움직이지 마세요 (“Please don’t move.”).
native_language_example: Don’t move when taking a photo.

meaning: “(Is that) what you want?” / “(That’s) what you want.”
additional_notes: 원하다 (“to want”) + -는 것 (“the thing that…”) + -이야/거야 (casual ‘is/it’s’). Often used in conversation to confirm or challenge someone’s intention: 그걸 원하는 거야? (“Is that what you want?”). With 뭘/대체 뭘 it can sound demanding or annoyed: 나한테 뭘 원하는 거야? (“What do you want from me?”). This form is casual/blunt; more polite alternatives include 원하는 거예요? / 원하시는 건가요?
native_language_example: Do you really want that?

additional_notes: 원하는 is the adjective form of 원하다 (“to want”), and 게 is a shortened form of 것(“thing”) with the subject marker -이/가 attached (것이 → 게). So 원하는 게 literally means “the wanted thing” = “what someone wants.” It’s very commonly followed by 뭐야/뭐예요/뭐죠? (“what is it?”) to ask someone’s intention or request: 원하는 게 뭐야? = “What do you want?” You can also add a person/topic before it (e.g., 내가/네가/그가 원하는 게…).
native_language_example: What do you want right now?

additional_notes: From 원하다 (to want) + -는 것 (thing that...) + 이/가 (subject marker). In speech, 것 + 이/가 often contracts to 게, so 원하는 게 = 원하는 것이/원하는 것이가. Commonly followed by 뭐(예요/야)? to ask “What do you want?” or used as a topic: 원하는 게 있으면 말해요 (“If you want something, tell me.”).
target_language_example: 원하는 게 있으면 저한테 말해 주세요.
native_language_example: If there’s something you want, please tell me.

additional_notes: Used when making a toast. Put a noun before it with 위해 (“for; in honor of”): 건강을 위해 건배! (“A toast to your health!”), 베르나르를 위해 건배! (“A toast to Bernard!”). Often said as “~을/를 위해 건배!”; you may also hear “~을/를 위해 건배합시다” (more polite: “Let’s toast to …”).
native_language_example: A toast to our friendship!

meaning: “What is …?” / “What’s …?” (casual, used after a noun ending in a consonant)
additional_notes:
Pattern: “X은 뭐야?” = “What is X?” where **은** is the topic marker used after a consonant-ending noun (e.g., 가방**은**). After a vowel-ending noun, use **는**: “X는 뭐야?”.

**뭐야** is informal/casual; polite equivalents include “뭐예요?” (or “뭐야?” ↔ “뭐예요?” depending on speech level).

Tone note: depending on context and intonation, it can sound neutral (“What is this?”) or more challenging/suspicious (“What is this supposed to be?”).
native_language_example: What’s this bag? / What is this bag?

meaning: “How is …?” / “What about …?” (asking for an opinion or how something is going).
additional_notes: Attach to a noun with the topic particle 은/는 (use 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel): X는/은 어때? Often asks for an evaluation (“How is X?”) or invites a suggestion/alternative (“How about X?”). This is casual; the more polite form is X는/은 어때요?
native_language_example: How is this restaurant? / What do you think of this restaurant?

additional_notes: Pattern: [noun + 은/는] + 어때요? (polite). Use it to ask someone’s opinion, evaluation, or condition about the topic noun: “How is the soup?”, “How about this option?”, “How is your father?”. Choose 은 after a consonant (국물은), and 는 after a vowel (동생은 is actually consonant ending ㅅ so 은; e.g., 날씨는). Often translates as “How about…?” when suggesting/considering an option, and “How is…?” when asking about status/quality.
native_language_example: How do you like this design?

meaning: “How was (it)?” (asking about a past experience, with the topic marked by 은/는).
additional_notes:
Use after a noun to ask someone’s opinion about something that already happened or that they already tried/experienced.
- Structure: [Noun + 은/는] + 어땠어? (casual / to friends)
- Choose 은 after a consonant (수업은), 는 after a vowel (여행은).
- Politer versions: 어땠어요? (polite), 어땠습니까? (formal).
- Often implies “How was it overall?” and can cover feelings, quality, and satisfaction depending on context.
native_language_example: How was the class?

additional_notes: Made from the topic particle 은/는 + 요 (polite ending). Attach it to a noun to ask about that item, often as a follow-up or to shift the focus: "X은요?" = "What about X?" / "How about X?" If the noun ends in a vowel, use "는요" instead (e.g., "이거는요?").
native_language_example: What about the price? / And the price?

meaning: "What about (X)?" / "As for (X)…?" (politely bringing up or asking about X).
additional_notes: Attached after a noun as the topic marker (은/는) + 요. Use it to ask about another person/thing in the same situation ("And what about X?") or to shift the topic to X. Choose 은 after a consonant (제목은요?), and 는 after a vowel (병원은요? actually ends in a consonant sound so it takes 은: 병원은요?). Often said with a questioning intonation and may be a shortened question (the rest is implied from context).
native_language_example: Then what about you?

meaning: “you bastard/you son of a bitch” (extremely vulgar insult).
additional_notes: A very aggressive swear used when yelling at someone in anger. 이 (“this”) + 개새끼 (a highly offensive insult; literally “dog’s offspring”) + 야 (vocative ending used when calling someone). Common in fights/threatening speech; avoid in polite conversation and most real-life situations. Not used toward friends jokingly unless the relationship is extremely close, and even then it’s risky.
target_language_example: 다시 건드리면 가만 안 둘 거야, 이 개새끼야.
native_language_example: Touch me again and I won’t let you get away with it, you bastard.

meaning: "You son of a bitch!" / "You bastard!" (a very strong insult).
additional_notes: A harsh profanity used when angrily insulting someone. Literally it’s like “this dog’s child,” but it functions as a strong swear word (similar in force to “son of a bitch”). The pattern “이 + (욕설) + 아” is used to call someone out directly. Avoid using it in polite situations; it can easily start a fight.
native_language_example: Hey, you bastard, get out right now!

meaning: "this guy / this one" (often slightly rude or scolding).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone/something close to the speaker (a person, animal, or even an object) when talking about them directly. It can sound like you’re scolding, annoyed, or speaking in a rough/teasing way, so avoid it in polite situations. Similar in feel to “this guy” / “this little punk” depending on tone.
target_language_example: 이 녀석 또 말 안 듣네.
native_language_example: This guy isn’t listening again.

additional_notes: Literally means “this dirty,” but in real speech it’s used to insult someone, usually before a noun like 놈/년/새끼 (“jerk/bastard/bitch,” etc.). It’s very rude and offensive—avoid using it except when recognizing it in arguments, movies, or subtitles.
native_language_example: Get lost, you dirty bastard!

additional_notes: A profanity used to curse or insult someone/something, placed before a noun (often a person-word): 이 망할 놈(아) “you damn bastard!”, 이 망할 자식(아) “you damn jerk!”, 이 망할 게… “this damn thing…”. Very aggressive and impolite—avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: 이 망할 놈아, 너 지금 뭐 하는 거야?
native_language_example: You damn idiot, what are you doing right now?

additional_notes: A rude insult used to scold or yell at someone (often in anger). Literally “this idiot,” but it functions like directly calling someone “idiot!” in English. Use with caution—can easily start a fight. (멍청아 is the insult; 이 adds emphasis like “you…”.)
target_language_example: 야, 이 멍청아! 그걸 왜 거기다 놨어?
native_language_example: Hey, you idiot! Why did you put that there?

additional_notes: Literally “this stupid …,” but it’s used as a shouted insult before a noun, often a swear/derogatory word (e.g., 자식, 놈, 새끼, 녀석). Very rude and aggressive—avoid in polite conversation. A much softer alternative is 멍청이야? (“Are you an idiot?”) or 바보야? (“Are you silly/idiot?”).
native_language_example: You idiot—why did you do that?

additional_notes: "이 문장" means "this sentence." The topic marker "-은/는" makes it "as for this sentence" or highlights it as the topic (often for comparison or explanation). Use "이 문장은 …" when asking about a meaning or giving an opinion about a specific sentence. Common patterns: "이 문장은 무슨 뜻이에요/인가요?" (What does this sentence mean?) and "이 문장은 괜찮은데…" (This sentence is okay, but…).
native_language_example: Does this sentence sound natural?

meaning: "this person" (the person near you / the person you mean).
additional_notes: Used to point out or refer to a specific person in the situation (often someone nearby or someone just mentioned). Common in questions like “이 사람 누구예요?” (“Who is this person?”). Depending on tone, it can also be used to address someone directly (“이 사람!”), which can sound like a mild scolding or “Hey, you.”
target_language_example: 저기요, 이 사람 여기 앉아도 돼요?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can this person sit here?

additional_notes: A highly aggressive swear used to insult someone (usually a man), often when angry or threatening. It can also be used toward someone you’re talking about (“Who is this bastard?”). Not appropriate in polite conversation; using it can start a fight. Common in dramas/movies, but learners should avoid saying it in real life.
native_language_example: This bastard is lying again.

meaning: “You bastard/you piece of shit” (a very strong insult).
additional_notes: Extremely rude profanity used to insult someone directly, often in anger or during a fight. 새끼 originally means “offspring,” but in this expression it’s a harsh slur; -야 is a casual/vocative ending used when calling someone. Avoid using this in real life (it can easily start a serious conflict).
native_language_example: Don’t lie, you bastard.

meaning: "this time" / "at this time" (this point in time).
additional_notes: Literally "this" (이) + "time/hour" (시간). Used to refer to the current time period or the time that is happening now. Often appears in phrases like "이 시간에" (at this time) or "이 시간쯤" (around this time). Depending on context, 시간 can mean either a general time period or a specific hour.
native_language_example: Is it okay to call at this time?

additional_notes: Used to point out the current (often late or early) time and express surprise, confusion, or mild disapproval. Common as a short question by itself (이 시간에?) and can be made polite with 요 (이 시간에요?).
native_language_example: You’re going out at this hour?

additional_notes: Points to a specific female person close by, visible, or already being talked about. 여자 can mean “woman” or (casually) “girl/young woman,” so the best translation depends on context. Often used when asking who she is (이 여자 누구죠?), what’s going on with her (이 여자 뭐야?), whether someone knows her (이 여자 아세요?), what you think of her (이 여자 어때?), or describing her (이 여자 엄청 예쁘다). Depending on tone, calling someone ‘이 여자’ can sound a bit blunt; using 그녀(‘she’) or 그 여자(‘that woman’) may fit better in some contexts.
native_language_example: What is this woman's name?

meaning: “this job/task/thing” (as the object of a verb).
additional_notes:
이 일 = “this work/this matter/this task.” 
이 일을 is 이 일 + object particle 을/를, so it’s used when “this job/task” is what you do, know, solve, etc. Common patterns: 이 일을 하다 (do this job), 이 일을 해결하다 (solve this matter), 이 일을 아는 사람 (someone who knows about this). Often paired with questions like 왜 (why), 어떻게 (how), 얼마 동안 (for how long).
target_language_example: 저는 이 일을 오늘 안에 끝내야 해요.
native_language_example: I have to finish this task by today.

meaning: “this bastard/jerk!” (an insulting way to refer to someone).
additional_notes: A harsh insult used when you’re angry, similar to “you bastard!” or “this guy!” (but ruder). Often used in confrontations or threats (e.g., with 죽여버리겠어 “I’ll kill you”). Literally means “this child/this son,” but it’s usually not about age or family—it's an insult. Avoid using it in polite conversation.
target_language_example: 이 자식, 어디서 그런 말을 해?
native_language_example: You jerk—how dare you say that?

additional_notes: A harsh way to address someone when you’re angry, similar to yelling “You jerk!” but stronger. Literally it comes from “this kid/this guy” + the vocative ending -아, but in real usage it’s an insult and can provoke a fight. You may hear it in arguments, movies, or when someone is threatening or cursing at another person. Avoid using it in real-life conversation.
native_language_example: Don’t lie, you bastard!

additional_notes: Used to refer to an amount, level, or degree that’s understood from context (often something you can see or just mentioned). Common patterns: 이 정도면… (“if it’s about this much/at this level, then…”), 이 정도로… (“to this extent/this much”). With 쯤(이)야 (as in 이 정도쯤이야), it can mean “this much is nothing / this is easy.”
native_language_example: If it’s about this much, it’s okay.

additional_notes: 이 = “this” + 집 = “house/home.” Depending on context, 이 집 can mean the physical house (“this house”) or the people who live there (“this household/family”). Often used with particles, e.g. 이 집은요? (“What about this house?”) or 이 집 사람이 아니다 (“not someone from this household”).
native_language_example: This house is our home.

additional_notes: 이 = “this” and 차 can mean either “car” or “tea.” In everyday conversation, 이 차 often means “this car,” especially when talking about ownership (이 차 당신 거예요? “Is this car yours?”) or pointing at a vehicle. Use context (topic, location, what you’re pointing at) to know whether it means car or tea. For extra clarity you can say 이 자동차 (this car) or 이 차(茶) (this tea; using the Chinese character is mostly in writing).
native_language_example: This car is my car.

additional_notes: 이 = “this”, 책 = “book”, -은 is the topic marker attached to 책 (so it becomes 책은). It’s used to introduce “this book” as the topic and often contrasts it with something else (e.g., “This book is easy, but that book is hard.”). In conversation or writing, what follows typically describes or evaluates the book.
native_language_example: This book is really interesting.

meaning: “(You mean) …?” / “…, please.” (polite, after a consonant-ending noun).
additional_notes: Attached to a noun that ends in a consonant (샘→샘이요, 선생님→선생님이요). Commonly used when repeating a word to confirm or ask for clarification: “당신이요?” = “Me?/You (said) you?”. It’s also used in requests/orders to politely state what you want: “두 개(가)요” / “물(이)요” = “Two, please / Water, please.” After a vowel-ending noun, you typically just use “요” (e.g., 커피요).
native_language_example: The teacher? I’ll explain it again for you.

additional_notes: Attached to a noun (especially one ending in a consonant) as a short, casual-polite way to state or confirm something. Very common when ordering or answering briefly: “아메리카노 한 잔이요.” = “An Americano, please.” In questions or retorts it can sound blunt/sassy: “진심이요?” = “Seriously?” Similar in function to “이에요” (more fully spelled-out). After vowel-ending nouns you usually just add “요” (e.g., “저요”).
native_language_example: I’m a student.

additional_notes: A casual command telling someone to release or stop holding something (or stop grabbing you). 놔 is the spoken contraction of 놓아 (from 놓다, “to let go/put down”). Can sound rude or aggressive depending on tone; use 제발 (“please”) to soften it (제발 이거 놔).
native_language_example: That hurts! Let go!

additional_notes: A casual way to get someone’s attention and show them something you’re holding or pointing to. Often said by itself (이거 봐!) or followed by a comment/question like 어때? (How is it?) or 예쁘지? (Isn’t it pretty?). You can repeat it for emphasis: 이거 봐, 이거!
native_language_example: Look at this—I made it myself.

additional_notes: Common in casual speech to strongly emphasize your reaction to “this” (이거). Often followed by a verb/adjective like 좋아(요) “(I) like (it),” 맛있어(요) “it’s tasty,” 예쁘다 “it’s pretty,” or commands like 봐봐 “look.” Similar in feeling to “This is really…” / “I seriously…” in English.
native_language_example: This is seriously delicious!

additional_notes: A conversational contraction of "이것은 내..." (or "이거는 내..."). It’s usually followed by a noun (내 가방) or by "꺼" to mean “mine” (이건 내 꺼야 = This is mine). "이건" is a casual spoken/written form; in more formal writing you may see "이것은".
native_language_example: This is my seat.

additional_notes: A common, casual reaction meaning “This is not acceptable” or “This is not the right way.” Literally from 이건 (= this + topic) + 아니다 (= is not). Often used to criticize a situation, decision, or behavior, like “No, this is wrong.”
target_language_example: 사람을 그렇게 대하는 건 이건 아니다.
native_language_example: Treating someone like that isn’t right.

meaning: “How about this?” / “What do you think of this?”
additional_notes: Used to suggest an idea or option and ask for the other person’s opinion. Very common in conversation when proposing something (“Then how about this?” = 그럼 이건 어때?). 이건 is a shortened form of 이것은 (“as for this”). Often said with a rising intonation as a question.
target_language_example: 시간이 없으면 내일 만나는 건 어때? 그럼 이건 어때?
native_language_example: If you don’t have time, how about meeting tomorrow? Then how about this?

meaning: "How do I/should I do this?" (with "this" as the object).
additional_notes:
Used when you’re asking for the method or way to handle something you’re pointing to or thinking of. "이걸" = "this" (object form of "이것"), and "어떻게" = "how". It’s usually followed by a verb: 
- 이걸 어떻게 해? = How do I do this?
- 이걸 어떻게 써? = How do I use this?
In casual speech, it can also sound like frustration: “How am I supposed to…?”
native_language_example: How do I use this?

additional_notes: 이걸 = “this” (object form of 이거). 왜 = “why.” Used at the start of a question to ask the reason for an action involving “this,” often followed by a verb: 이걸 왜 해? (Why do this?), 이걸 왜 줘요? (Why are you giving me this?). In casual speech it can sound annoyed or incredulous depending on tone.
native_language_example: Why do we have to do this now?

additional_notes: A casual way to get someone’s attention and direct them to what you’re showing (a thing, screen, photo, etc.). Often said with someone’s name (e.g., "민수야, 이것 봐!") or with "잠깐만" ("Wait a second—look at this!").
target_language_example: 이것 봐, 여기 사진 진짜 잘 나왔지?
native_language_example: Look at this—this photo came out really well, right?

meaning: “This, please” / “Look at this.” (used to get attention or ask for help with something).
additional_notes: Literally “this” + 좀 (“a bit”), but in everyday speech it’s often just a softener when asking someone to do something (like “please/just”). Common in requests: 이것 좀 봐 (Look at this), 이것 좀 들어봐/들어볼래? (Listen to this), 이것 좀 들어줘 (Hold this for me). On its own (이것 좀!) it can mean “Hey, look at this!” or “Excuse me—this!” depending on context and tone.
native_language_example: Wait a second—can you look at this for me?

meaning: “What is all this?” / “What is this all about?”
additional_notes: Literally “this + all,” used in questions to express surprise, confusion, or annoyance about a situation. Often followed by 뭐예요/뭡니까 (“what is it?”) or 무슨 일이죠 (“what’s going on?”).
native_language_example: What on earth is all this supposed to mean?

meaning: "What on earth is this…?" (strong emphasis: confusion/shock/annoyance).
additional_notes: Used before a question (often with 뭐/무슨/왜/어떻게) to strongly emphasize the speaker’s confusion or frustration. Very common in spoken Korean: 이게 대체 뭐야?/이게 대체 무슨 일이야? It’s more emotional than plain 이게 뭐예요?
target_language_example: 이게 대체 왜 이렇게 된 거야?
native_language_example: Why on earth did this end up like this?

meaning: "What is this…?" / "What kind of… is this?" (expressing surprise, confusion, or disapproval).
additional_notes: Used before a noun (일, 냄새, 뜻, 상황, 얘기, 짓, etc.) to react to something unexpected: 이게 무슨 + N(oun)? It often carries a tone like “What on earth…?” Depending on ending, it can be casual (이게 무슨 일이야?) or polite (이게 무슨 일입니까? / 이에요?).
native_language_example: What is this noise? / What are you talking about?

meaning: "What the heck are you doing?" / "What is this supposed to be?" (angry or shocked).
additional_notes: A very common spoken reaction when you’re upset, surprised, or disapproving of what someone did. Literally “What act/deed is this?” (이게=this + 무슨=what kind of + 짓=act/deed + -이야=casual ‘is’). Often said to someone directly (Name + 이게 무슨 짓이야?) or to the situation. Casual/informal; in polite speech you can say "이게 무슨 짓이에요?" or more strongly "이게 무슨 짓입니까?"
target_language_example: 야, 이게 무슨 짓이야? 지금 당장 그만해.
native_language_example: Hey, what the heck are you doing? Stop it right now.

meaning: "What is this?" / "What’s going on?" (often expressing surprise or annoyance).
additional_notes: Very common informal spoken phrase. Literally "this (이게) + what (뭐) + is (야)". Depending on tone, it can be a neutral question (이게 뭐야?) or an exclamation of shock/irritation (이게 뭐야!). For a more polite version, use "이게 뭐예요?" or "이게 뭔가요?".
target_language_example: 어? 이게 뭐야? 내 지갑이 없어.
native_language_example: Huh? What’s going on? My wallet is gone.

additional_notes: Used to ask what something is (an object, a situation, a sound, etc.). 이게 is a shortened form of 이것이 (“this” as the subject). 뭐죠 is a polite/soft form of 뭐예요?/뭐야? (“what is it?”). Often said with surprise: “But what is this?”
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is this?

meaning: "How is this…?" / "How could this…?" (often expressing disbelief).
additional_notes: Starts a question about a surprising or hard-to-believe situation. Common patterns: "이게 어떻게 + N(이/가) …?" (How is this N…?) and "이게 어떻게 된 거야?" (What happened?/How did this happen?). Often sounds like the speaker is shocked, upset, or incredulous rather than calmly asking for information.
native_language_example: How did this end up coming all the way here?

meaning: (Why are you) acting like this? / (Why are you) doing this?
additional_notes: Usually used with 왜 (“why”) to question someone’s behavior, often sounding annoyed, upset, or confused. It’s the spoken, casual style of 이러다 (“to act/be like this”) + -는 거야 (explaining/insisting tone). Can refer to someone’s words, attitude, or actions in the moment.
target_language_example: 갑자기 소리 지르지 마. 왜 이러는 거야?
native_language_example: Don’t suddenly yell. Why are you acting like this?

additional_notes: A very common spoken phrase used to tell someone to stop what they’re doing (often because it’s inappropriate, dangerous, embarrassing, or upsetting). It’s informal (반말). More polite alternatives: "이러지 마세요" or "그러지 마세요." Literally means “don’t act/do like this.”
target_language_example: 제발 이러지 마. 우리 얘기 좀 하자.
native_language_example: Please stop it. Let’s talk.

meaning: 'something like this' / 'this kind of thing' (as the object of the verb).
additional_notes: Spoken contraction of "이런 것(을)": 이런 = "this kind of," 것 = "thing," and 걸 = 것을 (object-marked form used in speech/writing). Used when reacting to a situation/object and referring to it as "this sort of thing".
native_language_example: Who taught you something like this?

meaning: "this kind of thing" / "something like this (happening)" (often as the subject of a sentence).
additional_notes: Formed from 이런 (“this kind of”) + 일 (“thing; event”) + 이 (subject marker). It’s commonly used when reacting to a situation, often with verbs like 있다/없다 (to exist/happen), 생기다 (to occur), or 모르다 (to not know): e.g., "이런 일이 있을 줄 몰랐어요" (“I didn’t know something like this would happen”). In casual speech, the subject marker 이 may be dropped: "이런 일 처음이야".
native_language_example: I didn’t know something like this would happen.

meaning: “something like this/this kind of thing” (often while pointing to or referring to something).
additional_notes: Literally “this kind of thing” (이런 = “like this/this kind of” + 거 = “thing” in casual speech; more formal: 것). Used to refer to an item, situation, or idea that’s present or obvious from context. Can be a full question by itself (이런 거?) meaning “Something like this?” or “This kind of thing?” Often paired with verbs like 보다 (to see), 좋아하다 (to like), 하다/해주다 (to do/do for someone), 있다 (to have).
native_language_example: I’ve never seen something like this before.

additional_notes: Used when pointing to or referring to an example of a type of thing, situation, or behavior. Often comes up when showing someone an item or giving an example (e.g., 'things like this'). You can also use it more generally without literally pointing at something.
native_language_example: Do you like this kind of thing?

meaning: "(How) can this happen?" / "Can it be like this?"
additional_notes: A fragment meaning “this kind of thing can/could happen,” usually followed by 있다/없다 (e.g., 이럴 수가 있어요? 이럴 수가 없어요). Very commonly used as the fixed exclamation 이럴 수가! to show shock, disbelief, or frustration (similar to “No way!” / “How is this possible?!”).
target_language_example: 이럴 수가! 또 지갑을 집에 두고 왔어.
native_language_example: No way! I left my wallet at home again.

meaning: “This can happen.” / “It’s possible for this to happen.”
additional_notes: Conversational phrase used when reacting to a surprising or disappointing situation, often with a feeling of disbelief or resignation (similar to “How can this happen?”). It can also be said as a question: “이럴 수 있어?” (“Can this happen?” / “Is this for real?”). More formal/polite: “이럴 수 있어요.”
target_language_example: 시험에 또 떨어졌어… 이럴 수 있어?
native_language_example: I failed the exam again… How can this happen?

meaning: "How could this happen?!" / "How can it be like this?!" (shock, disbelief, outrage).
additional_notes: An exclamation used when something is surprising, unbelievable, or unfair. Often appears with intensifiers like 어떻게/도대체 (e.g., "어떻게 이럴 수가 있어?"), and is usually rhetorical (you’re not really asking for an explanation). It comes from "이렇다" (to be like this) + "-ㄹ 수" (can) + subject marker "가"—literally, "can it be like this?"
target_language_example: 이럴 수가… 내가 열심히 준비했는데 떨어졌어.
native_language_example: How could this happen… I studied so hard, but I failed.

meaning: “ended up like this / became like this.”
additional_notes: From 되다 (“to become”) + the modifier ending -(으)ㄴ, so it describes a noun: “the (thing/situation) that became like this.” Common in questions about how a situation happened: 어쩌다 이렇게 된 거야? (“How did it end up like this?”). Often used with 것 (건/거): 이렇게 된 거(야/인데), and with 지 to mean “since it became like this”: 이렇게 된 지 얼마나 됐어? (“How long has it been like this?”).
native_language_example: Why did it end up like this?

meaning: to do it like this; to do it this way.
additional_notes: Used when showing or explaining a method (often while demonstrating). 이렇게 means “like this / this way,” and 하다 means “to do.” You’ll also hear variations like 그렇게 하다 (“do it that way”) and 저렇게 하다 (“do it that way over there”).
target_language_example: 이렇게 하세요. 아니면 제가 이렇게 하다 보일까요?
native_language_example: Do it like this. Or should I show you by doing it like this?

additional_notes: 이름(“name”) + 은 (topic marker). It sets “name” as the topic, often to ask or confirm a name. Common full forms: 이름은 뭐예요? (polite) / 이름은 뭐야? (casual) = “What’s your name?” It can also be used alone (이름은?) as a shortened question meaning “And your name?” depending on context.
native_language_example: What’s your name?

meaning: "How (do/did you) know the name…?" / "How (do/did you) call (someone) by name…?"
additional_notes: A common sentence starter meaning “(someone’s) name + how…?”. 이름 is “name,” and -을 marks it as the object. It’s most often followed by verbs like 알다 (to know) or 부르다 (to call): 내 이름을 어떻게 알아요? = “How do you know my name?” You can swap in another person’s name: 걔 이름을 어떻게 알았어? = “How did you know his/her name?”
native_language_example: How did you know my name?

additional_notes: A casual way to ask someone’s name, often to a friend or someone younger. Literally “(your) name is what?”. You’ll also hear/see: “너 이름이 뭐니?”, “네 이름이 뭐니?” (same meaning), or the more polite “이름이 뭐예요?/이름이 뭐야?”. Using “야,” before it can sound more abrupt (like “Hey,”).
native_language_example: We’re meeting for the first time—what’s your name?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s name or the name of something (a hotel, club, etc.). Very casual speech; with strangers, use the polite form “이름이 뭐예요?” or “성함이 어떻게 되세요?” for extra politeness. Often said as “(너/네) 이름이 뭐야?” (your name) or “(이거/그거) 이름이 뭐야?” (what is this called?).
native_language_example: What’s that store’s name?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask someone’s name, or the name of a person/animal mentioned in context. You can specify whose name by adding a noun before it (e.g., 개/남편/환자 이름이 뭐죠?). Literally “(The) name is what?” and uses the polite ending -죠 (softer than direct -예요/-입니까 in many situations).
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s your name?

meaning: “What’s the name?” / “What was it called again?”
additional_notes: A casual way to ask for the name of a person, animal, place, or thing. Literally “(the) name + subject marker 이 + 뭐지 (what is it?)”. Often used when you’re trying to remember a name. More polite: 이름이 뭐예요?/이름이 뭐죠?
native_language_example: What’s that actor’s name again?

meaning: to come here / come this way.
additional_notes: 이리 means “here/this way” (a slightly more directional “here” than 여기). With 오다 (“to come”), it’s often used in commands, where 오다 conjugates: 이리 와 (casual), 이리 와요 (polite), 이리 오세요 (polite, more formal). The dictionary form 이리 오다 is also used in narration, explanations, quotes, or instructions.
target_language_example: 사진 찍기 전에 이리 오다부터 하고, 여기서 같이 서요.
native_language_example: Before taking a picture, first come here, and stand here together.

additional_notes: A casual command telling someone to come toward the speaker (“come this way/over here”). Often used when calling someone closer (kids, friends, pets). Softer/polite alternatives: 이리 오세요 (“Please come here”), 여기로 와/와 줘 (“Come here / come here for me”).
target_language_example: 잠깐만, 이리 와. 이거 좀 봐.
native_language_example: Wait a second—come here. Look at this.

additional_notes: An informal command meaning “give it to me (here).” Often said strongly or urgently, like when grabbing something away. You can add the object: "(그거) 이리 줘" (“Give me that.”). To sound a bit softer, say "이리 줘 봐" (“Let me see / give it to me for a second”) or add "좀" ("이리 줘 좀").
native_language_example: I’ll take a look at it. Give it here.

additional_notes: 이상하다 means “to be strange/weird.” 거 is a casual spoken form of 것 (“thing”), so 이상한 거 often sounds conversational. It’s used to refer to an unspecified weird thing or event you saw, heard, have, etc. Common with verbs like 보다 (to see) and 가지고 있다 (to have). Depending on context, it can mean simply “weird” or more like “fishy/suspicious.”
target_language_example: 어제 밤에 밖에서 이상한 거 들었어.
native_language_example: I heard something weird outside last night.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop or to suggest ending something. Often followed by a verb (e.g., 이제 그만 가자/갈까 “shall we go now?”) or used alone as a firm “That’s enough.” Can sound strong depending on tone; you can soften it with polite endings (e.g., 이제 그만하세요).
native_language_example: Let’s stop talking about it now.

additional_notes: Used to ask what to do next, often when you’re unsure, finished with something, or need instructions. It commonly continues with a verb like 하다/할 거다/해야 하다 (e.g., 이제 뭘 하지? / 이제 뭘 할 거야? / 이제 뭘 해야 해요?). 뭘 is a shortened form of 뭐를 (“what” + object marker 를).
target_language_example: 다 끝났어. 이제 뭘 하면 돼?
native_language_example: I’m done. What should I do now?

meaning: “So what do we do now?” / “What happens now?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what the next step is from this point (“now”), often when you’re unsure, stuck, or waiting for instructions. It can be followed by verbs like 하다 (“do”) or 되다 (“become/happen”): 이제 어떻게 할 거야? (What will you do now?), 이제 어떻게 되는 거야? (What’s going to happen now?). Politeness changes with the ending: 해요/하죠 (polite), 해? (casual), 합니까? (formal).
native_language_example: A problem came up—so what do we do now?

meaning: “Now what (are we going to do)?” / “What are you going to do now?”
additional_notes: A shortened, conversational form of "이제 어쩌(면)" or "이제 어쩔 거야/거지/거죠?" It’s used when reacting to a situation and asking what the next step is—often with a feeling of worry, frustration, or pressure (similar to English “Now what?”). It’s usually followed by "거야?" (casual), "거지?" (casual, often expecting agreement), or "거죠?" (polite).
native_language_example: The buses stopped running. Now what are we going to do?

meaning: "now (of all times)" / "at this point" (often: too late or after everything that's happened).
additional_notes: Used to criticize or express disbelief/frustration that someone is doing or saying something only now, after the situation has already progressed. Often appears in rhetorical questions or scolding: 이제 와서 + (verb/statement)? / 이제 와서 + 하지 마(요). Nuance: 'Why bring that up now?' 'You’re saying that now?'
native_language_example: Saying you’re sorry now doesn’t help.

meaning: "Now we…" / "So now, what about us…?" (a lead-in to what happens next or your relationship).
additional_notes: Literally "now" (이제) + "we/us" (우리). It’s commonly used at the start of a sentence to set up the next situation: worries about what to do (이제 우리 어쩌지?), dramatic predictions (이제 우리 죽는다!), or asking about the status of a relationship (이제 우리 친구야?). Often followed by a question, exclamation, or suggestion.
native_language_example: So where do we go now?

additional_notes: A common sentence fragment meaning “now, home…”. It’s usually followed by a verb like 가다 (“to go”) or 갈 수 있다 (“can go”): 이제 집에 가요 (“I’m going home now”). 이제 = “now / from now on,” and 집에 uses -에 to mean “to/at (a place)” depending on the verb.
native_language_example: You can go home now.

meaning: (as in 이해가 돼요/안 돼요) 'I understand' / 'it makes sense' (or 'I don’t').
additional_notes: Usually used with 되다 (to become): 이해가 돼요 = 'I understand' / 'That makes sense.' Negative: 이해가 안 돼요 = 'I don’t understand' / 'That doesn’t make sense.' Often appears in questions like 이해가 돼? ('Do you get it?'). By itself, 이해 means 'understanding,' and -가 is the subject marker.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I still don’t understand.

additional_notes: A very common spoken fragment, usually completed as **이해가 안 돼요** (polite) or **이해가 안 돼** (casual). Often followed by what you don’t understand: **이해가 안 돼요** / **이해가 안 돼요, 왜 그런지** (“I don’t understand why…”).
target_language_example: 죄송한데, 이 부분이 이해가 안 돼요.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don’t understand this part.

additional_notes: Very common spoken, casual expression. Literally means “understanding doesn’t work/doesn’t happen,” but it’s used like “I don’t get it.” Often said alone, or followed by questions like 왜? (why?) or 뭐야? (what is it?). With rising intonation (이해가 안 돼?) it can mean “You don’t understand?” or “You don’t get it?” depending on context. Politer alternatives: 이해가 안 돼요, 이해가 안 됩니다.
target_language_example: 미안한데, 그 규칙은 아직 이해가 안 돼.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I still don’t understand that rule.

additional_notes: Made from 일 (work) + 안 (not). It’s used right before a verb, most commonly 하다: 일 안 해요 (I’m not working / I don’t work). Often used in questions or scolding like 빨리 일 안 해? (“Aren’t you working? Hurry up.”). In writing, it’s commonly spaced as 일 안 해요/일 안 하고.
target_language_example: 지금 일 안 하고 뭐 해요?
native_language_example: If you’re not working right now, what are you doing?

additional_notes: 일 means “work” or “job.” The particle -은 marks it as the topic, often when switching topics or asking/checking about someone’s work situation: “일은 괜찮아?” (“How’s work?”). It can also be used alone as a short question (“일은?” = “And work?” / “What about work?”). In exclamations like “그런 일은!”, it’s usually an incomplete sentence meaning something like “Such a thing (can’t happen)!” / “No way!”—the rest is implied.
native_language_example: How’s work these days?

additional_notes: Casual/informal past-tense question used when you sense something happened (often something bad or unusual). Commonly appears as 무슨 일 있었어? or 뭔 일 있었어? (= shortened 무슨). Polite version: 일 있었어요? / 무슨 일 있었어요?
target_language_example: 얼굴이 안 좋아 보이는데, 무슨 일 있었어?
native_language_example: You don’t look well—did something happen?

meaning: 'can get up' / 'able to get up (stand up)'.
